summary: An informational memo proposing a new naming plan for directory-enabled applications, noting that the usual X.500 naming approach has been an obstacle to wide deployment. It builds on strengths of widely used naming systems.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 2377 proposes naming directory entries with familiar Internet names. It uses registered DNS names for the upper levels and allows existing identifiers, such as a mailbox identifier, to name individual entries.

subtitle: A directory naming plan that builds on registered domain names and existing identifiers.

tldr.problem: The authors say conventional X.500 naming was difficult to deploy because organization names required registration and common names could collide.
tldr.mechanism: The plan builds the upper levels of directory names from DNS domain components and suggests uid or cn for leaf entries.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2377 is Informational, not a standard, and was updated by RFC 4519.

today: RFC 2377 is an Informational memo and was updated by RFC 4519. It has not been obsoleted according to the batch metadata.

sections.title: The Proposed Naming Plan
sections.content:
The memo proposes an alternative or extension to conventional X.500 naming for Internet directory services. It has two main parts: build the upper levels of the directory hierarchy from DNS names, and provide choices for naming entries at the leaves.

The plan is optional. The authors encourage directory software developers to expect that it may be used.
sections.plainLanguage: The proposal reuses names that organizations already have on the Internet. It sets out a way to use those names for directory branches and to choose names for entries below them.

sections.title: Why the Authors Proposed a Change
sections.content:
The authors report that common names can collide when many people are listed under one directory node. Making each common name unique may require extra information and create long names.

They also describe organization-name registration as difficult and cumbersome. The memo says these issues contributed to the slow growth of the Internet X.500 Directory Pilot, which had about 1.5 million entries at the time.
sections.plainLanguage: Many people can have the same name, so a directory needs another way to distinguish them. The authors also wanted to avoid relying on a separate process to register every organization name.

sections.title: Requirements for Directory Names
sections.content:
The plan seeks names that are unambiguous within a directory context and hierarchical enough to support delegation and division of directory information across servers. It also aims to work with LDAP and loosely connected directory servers.

Other goals are to reuse existing Internet naming systems and to use information that a person can recognize in their own distinguished name. The RFC does not attempt to create one global namespace for every directory object.
sections.plainLanguage: Names should identify entries within their directory, support delegation, and work across connected servers. The plan also aims to reuse familiar names without claiming that every directory shares one universal list.

sections.title: Building Directory Names
sections.content:
The domain component attribute, dc, represents the labels of a registered domain name. For example, the memo gives dc=acme, dc=com for the domain acme.com. A subdomain can add another directory level.

Leaf entries can use uid or cn. The authors suggest using an existing identifier such as a mailbox identifier for a person where suitable, and using a common name for other entries. Applications must not assume that every uid value is a working mailbox.
sections.plainLanguage: A domain such as acme.com can become directory levels named dc=acme and dc=com. An entry below those levels can use a user identifier or a common name.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Directory access controls can prevent unauthorized clients from browsing parts of a directory tree. The RFC warns that DNS queries may still reveal names or structure in protected parts of the tree.

Making some directory information public may help others infer the names and structure of less visible entries.
sections.plainLanguage: Access controls can restrict who browses directory entries. Public DNS information may still reveal clues about names or directory structure.
